lessons.title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Power
lessons.description: The different energy stores, how energy is transferred between them, and what power means.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Stores

In physics, energy is described as being held in different energy stores. Energy is never created or destroyed — it is simply transferred from one store to another. This principle is known as the conservation of energy.

You need to know eight energy stores. Each one describes a different way that energy can be held within a system.

Key Fact

The eight energy stores are: kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational potential, elastic potential, electrostatic, magnetic, and nuclear. You must be able to identify which stores are involved in any energy transfer scenario.

Kinetic energy is the energy store of any moving object. A car on a motorway, a sprinter in a race, and air molecules in a warm room all have energy in their kinetic store.

Thermal energy is associated with the temperature of an object. The hotter something is, the more energy it has in its thermal store. When you heat water in a kettle, energy is transferred to the thermal store of the water.

Chemical energy is the energy stored in chemical bonds. Food, fuels such as petrol and natural gas, and batteries all store energy chemically. This energy is released during chemical reactions.

Gravitational potential energy (GPE) is the energy stored by an object that has been raised above the ground. The higher the object, the greater its mass, and the stronger the gravitational field, the more GPE it has.

Elastic potential energy is stored in objects that have been stretched or compressed, such as springs, rubber bands, and trampolines. When the object returns to its original shape, this energy is released.

Electrostatic energy is stored when electric charges are separated. Magnetic energy is stored when magnets are pushed together or pulled apart. Nuclear energy is stored in the nuclei of atoms and released during nuclear reactions such as fission and fusion.

Energy Transfers

Energy can be transferred between stores in four main ways, known as energy transfer pathways. These are: mechanically (when a force acts on an object), electrically (when charge flows through a circuit), by heating (when there is a temperature difference), and by radiation (such as light waves or sound waves).

For example, when a ball is dropped from a height: energy is transferred from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store as the ball falls (mechanically, by the force of gravity). When the ball hits the ground, some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the ball and the ground (by heating), and some to the surroundings as sound (by radiation).

Key Fact

Energy is always conserved. In a closed system, the total energy before a transfer equals the total energy after. Energy that seems to “disappear” has actually been transferred to less useful stores — usually the thermal store of the surroundings.

In any transfer, some energy is dissipated (spread out) into less useful stores, usually as thermal energy in the surroundings. This is why no energy transfer is 100% efficient in practice. A light bulb, for example, is supplied with energy electrically from the mains. It transfers that energy to light (useful) and to the thermal store of the surroundings (wasted).

Calculating Kinetic Energy

The amount of kinetic energy an object has depends on its mass and speed. The equation is:

\(Kinetic energy = \frac{1}{2} \times mass \times speed^{2}\)
Ek = ½ mv²

Where Ek is kinetic energy in joules (J), m is mass in kilograms (kg), and v is speed in metres per second (m/s). Notice that speed is squared — this means doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

Question: A car has a mass of 1200 kg and travels at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

Answer: Ek = ½ × 1200 × 15² = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J (or 135 kJ).

Calculating Gravitational Potential Energy

Gravitational potential energy depends on the mass of the object, the gravitational field strength, and the height above the ground:

\(GPE = mass \times \text{gravitational field strength} \times height\)
Ep = mgh

Where Ep is gravitational potential energy in joules (J), m is mass in kilograms (kg), g is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N/kg) — on Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg — and h is height in metres (m).

Question: A 0.5 kg ball is held 4 m above the ground. Calculate its gravitational potential energy. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

Answer: Ep = 0.5 × 9.8 × 4 = 19.6 J.

Elastic Potential Energy

When a spring is stretched or compressed within its limit of proportionality, it stores elastic potential energy. The equation is:

\(Elastic \text{potential energy} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{spring constant} \times extension^{2}\)
Ee = ½ ke²

Where Ee is elastic potential energy in joules (J), k is the spring constant in newtons per metre (N/m), and e is the extension in metres (m). Like kinetic energy, extension is squared — doubling the extension quadruples the energy stored.

Work Done and Energy Transfer

Work done is the scientific term for energy transfer. When a force causes an object to move through a distance, work is done on that object. The equation is:

\(Work done = force \times distance\)
W = Fs

Where W is work done in joules (J), F is force in newtons (N), and s is distance along the line of action of the force in metres (m). One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre.

Key Fact

Work done = energy transferred. These two quantities are always equal. If 500 J of work is done on an object, then 500 J of energy has been transferred. The unit for both is the joule (J).

Power

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, or equivalently the rate at which work is done. A more powerful device transfers the same amount of energy in less time. The equations are:

\(Power = \text{energy transferred} \div time\)
P = E/t

\(Power = \text{work done} \div time\)
P = W/t

Power is measured in watts (W). One watt means one joule of energy is transferred per second. A 60 W light bulb transfers 60 joules of energy every second. For larger values, kilowatts (kW) are used: 1 kW = 1000 W.

Question: A motor transfers 15,000 J of energy in 5 minutes. Calculate its power.

Answer: First convert time: 5 minutes = 300 seconds. Then P = E/t = 15,000 ÷ 300 = 50 W.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Combined Science, calculation questions on energy are very common. Always show your working clearly: write the equation, substitute values with units, and give your final answer with the correct unit (J for energy, W for power). Watch out for unit conversions — time must be in seconds for power calculations, and speed must be in m/s for kinetic energy. In “explain” questions about energy transfers, name the specific energy stores (not just “energy”) and state how the energy is transferred between them.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are eight energy stores (kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational potential, elastic potential, electrostatic, magnetic, nuclear) and four transfer pathways (mechanically, electrically, by heating, by radiation).
  • Key equations: Ek = ½mv², Ep = mgh, Ee = ½ke², W = Fs, and P = E/t. You must be able to select and apply the correct equation for each scenario.
  • Energy is always conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. Dissipated energy (usually thermal) is wasted, not lost.

practice_questions.text: Describe the energy transfers that occur when a car brakes and comes to a stop. Explain why the brakes get hot and discuss the implications of the conservation of energy in this situation.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed, well-organised response that correctly identifies energy stores and transfer pathways, explains heating of brakes, and links to conservation of energy with appropriate terminology.
Indicative content:
• The car has energy in its kinetic store while moving (1)
• When the brakes are applied, friction acts between the brake pads and disc (1)
• Work is done by friction, transferring energy from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes (1)
• The brakes get hot because the thermal energy store of the brake pads and discs increases (1)
• The car slows down as its kinetic energy decreases (1)
• Energy is conserved — the kinetic energy lost equals the thermal energy gained by the brakes and surroundings (1)
• The thermal energy is dissipated to the surroundings and cannot easily be recovered for useful purposes (1)
Mid band (3-4): Identifies key energy stores and explains why brakes get hot, but may lack detail on conservation of energy or dissipation.
Lower band (1-2): Basic reference to energy transfer with limited explanation or incorrect store names.

The energy store associated with the temperature of an object — the hotter it is, the more energy is in its thermal store.

The energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object such as a spring or rubber band.
The four ways energy moves between stores: mechanically (by a force), electrically (by a current), by heating, or by radiation (light or sound waves).
Energy that is transferred to stores that are not useful — typically the thermal store of the surroundings, often described as wasted energy.

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources
lessons.description: Conservation of energy, calculating efficiency, and comparing renewable and non-renewable resources.
lessons.content_html:
The Principle of Conservation of Energy

One of the most important ideas in physics is the conservation of energy. This principle states that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another, or dissipated to the surroundings. The total amount of energy in a closed system always stays the same.

A closed system is one where energy cannot enter or leave. An insulated flask of hot water is a good example — the thermal energy stays inside the flask because the insulation prevents transfer to the surroundings. In a closed system, any energy transferred away from one store must appear in another store.

Key Fact

Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores. In a closed system, the total energy before a transfer is always equal to the total energy afterwards.

Energy Transfers and Dissipation

When energy is transferred, some of it usually ends up in stores that are not useful. This energy is said to be dissipated (or “wasted”). Dissipated energy is transferred to the thermal energy store of the surroundings, where it spreads out and becomes increasingly difficult to use.

Consider a light bulb. Electrical energy is transferred to the light’s thermal and light energy stores. The light is useful, but the heat given off is wasted energy. The wasted thermal energy heats the surroundings and cannot easily be recovered. This is why no device is ever 100% efficient in practice.

A bungee jumper standing on a platform has energy in the gravitational potential energy store. As they fall, this transfers to the kinetic energy store. When the bungee cord stretches, kinetic energy transfers to the elastic potential energy store of the cord. At each stage, some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings through air resistance and stretching of the cord. The total energy remains the same throughout.

Engineers design systems to minimise dissipation. Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts, so less energy is wasted as heat. Thermal insulation (such as loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, double glazing, and draught excluders) reduces unwanted thermal energy transfer from buildings. In a house, the biggest heat losses occur through the roof and walls, so insulating these areas has the greatest impact.

Calculating Efficiency

Efficiency tells us how good a device is at transferring energy usefully. It compares the useful output energy (or power) to the total input energy (or power).

The equation is:

\(Efficiency = \text{useful output energy transfer} \div \text{total input energy transfer}\)

This gives a decimal between 0 and 1. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage. You can also use power instead of energy:

\(Efficiency = \text{useful output power} \div \text{total input power}\)

Key Fact

Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy. It can never be greater than 1 (100%) because energy is always dissipated. A higher efficiency means less energy is wasted.

A motor has a total input energy of 500 J and transfers 350 J usefully to the kinetic energy store of a load. Calculate its efficiency.

Step 1: Write the equation: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
Step 2: Substitute: Efficiency = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70.
Step 3: Convert to percentage: 0.70 × 100 = 70%.
This means 70% of the energy is usefully transferred and 30% is dissipated (wasted).

Energy Resources — Renewable and Non-Renewable

The world relies on a mix of renewable and non-renewable energy resources to generate electricity, heat buildings, and power transport. You need to know the advantages and disadvantages of each type.

Non-Renewable Resources

Fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas) are the most widely used non-renewable resources. They were formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms. Burning them releases carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change) and sulphur dioxide (which causes acid rain).

Nuclear energy uses uranium or plutonium as fuel. Nuclear power stations produce no greenhouse gases during operation, and a small amount of fuel produces a large amount of energy. However, they are expensive to build and decommission, and used fuel rods produce radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years. The 1986 Chernobyl disaster highlighted the dangers of nuclear accidents.

Key Fact

Non-renewable resources will run out. The three fossil fuels are coal, oil, and natural gas. Nuclear fuel (uranium/plutonium) is also non-renewable. Fossil fuels release CO2 (global warming) and SO2 (acid rain).

Renewable Resources

Renewable resources will not run out because they are replenished naturally. Most produce no greenhouse gases during operation, but they each have limitations.

Wind power: Wind turns turbine blades, transferring kinetic energy to electrical energy via a generator. Wind power produces no CO2, but turbines only generate electricity when the wind blows — making them unreliable. Some people also consider them unsightly or noisy.

Solar power: Solar cells convert sunlight directly into electricity. Solar panels are renewable and cost nothing to run once installed, but they depend on sunlight and produce no electricity at night or on very cloudy days.

Hydroelectric power: Rainwater is collected in a reservoir and released downhill through turbines to generate electricity. It produces no CO2 during operation and can respond quickly to changes in demand. However, building the dam requires flooding a valley, which destroys habitats.

Tidal power: Water trapped at high tide is released through turbines to generate electricity. Tidal power is highly reliable because tides are predictable, but barrages can harm marine wildlife and are expensive to build. Tidal power is driven by the gravitational pull of the Moon, not by energy from the Sun.

Geothermal power: Water is pumped down into hot rocks deep underground and returns as steam to turn turbines. It is only available in volcanic areas or places with hot rocks near the surface, which limits where it can be used.

Biomass: Fuel made from living or recently living organisms (such as wood, animal waste, or crops). Biomass is considered carbon neutral because the CO2 released when burned equals the CO2 the organisms absorbed during growth. However, growing and transporting biomass does have a carbon footprint.

Trends in Energy Use

The UK is shifting from fossil fuels towards renewable sources. Demand for electricity varies throughout the day and across seasons — it peaks in the evening and in winter. Fossil fuel and nuclear power stations provide reliable base load supply. Hydroelectric and gas-fired power stations can start up quickly to meet sudden increases in demand. Renewable sources like wind and solar contribute a growing share but cannot always guarantee supply because they depend on weather conditions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In energy questions, always state which energy store energy is being transferred from and to (e.g. “from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the surroundings”). For efficiency calculations, show every step: write the equation, substitute values, then give your answer as a decimal and a percentage. When comparing energy resources, structure your answer with clear advantages and disadvantages of each — and always link your points to reliability, environmental impact, or cost.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is always conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. Dissipated energy spreads to the thermal store of the surroundings and is no longer useful.
  • Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy. No device can be 100% efficient because some energy is always dissipated. Lubrication and insulation reduce unwanted transfers.
  • Non-renewable resources (fossil fuels, nuclear) will run out and fossil fuels release greenhouse gases. Renewable resources (wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass) won’t run out but many are weather-dependent and unreliable.

lessons.title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference
lessons.description: Ohm’s law, V=IR calculations, and I-V characteristics of resistors, lamps and diodes.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Current, Resistance and Potential Difference?

Every electrical circuit relies on three linked quantities. Current is the flow of electrical charge around a circuit. It is measured in amperes (A) using an ammeter, which is always connected in series — in line with the component being tested.

Potential difference (p.d.) is the energy transferred per unit of charge that passes between two points. It is measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter, which is always connected in parallel — across the component.

Resistance is a measure of how much a component opposes the flow of current. It is measured in ohms (Ω). The higher the resistance, the harder it is for current to flow.

Key Fact

In most circuits the charge carriers are electrons. Conventional current flows from positive to negative, but electrons actually move from negative to positive.

Ohm’s Law

The relationship between potential difference, current and resistance is given by the equation:

\(\text{potential difference} = current \times resistance\)

\(V = I \times R\)

where V is potential difference in volts, I is current in amperes, and R is resistance in ohms. You need to be able to rearrange this equation: \(I = V \div R\) and \(R = V \div I\).

This equation applies to all components, but Ohm’s law specifically states that for some conductors, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference — provided the temperature remains constant. A component that behaves this way is called an ohmic conductor because its resistance stays the same regardless of the current flowing through it. A fixed resistor at constant temperature is a good example.

Key Fact

V = IR is the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance. Ohm’s law is the statement that current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature — this only applies to ohmic conductors.

Question: A resistor has a resistance of 15 Ω. The current flowing through it is 0.4 A. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.

Answer: V = I × R = 0.4 × 15 = 6.0 V

Question: A lamp has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 2.5 A flowing through it. Calculate the resistance.

Answer: R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 2.5 = \(4.8 \, \Omega\)

Investigating I–V Characteristics

One of your required practicals asks you to investigate the I–V characteristics of different circuit components. The basic circuit uses a variable power supply (or a battery with a variable resistor), an ammeter in series, a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and the component itself.

You change the potential difference using the variable supply, record the ammeter and voltmeter readings at each setting, then reverse the connections and repeat for negative values. Plotting current (y-axis) against potential difference (x-axis) gives an I–V characteristic graph. The shape of this graph tells you about the component’s behaviour.

I–V Graphs for Key Components

Ohmic conductor (fixed resistor at constant temperature): The graph is a straight line through the origin. This means current is directly proportional to potential difference — doubling the p.d. doubles the current. The resistance is constant and can be calculated from the gradient.

Filament lamp: The graph is a curve that starts steep and flattens out. As current increases, the filament heats up and its resistance increases. At higher p.d. values, the same increase in voltage produces a smaller increase in current. The graph is symmetrical — reversing the p.d. gives the same shape in the opposite direction.

Diode: A diode allows current to flow in only one direction. In the forward direction, current flows once the p.d. reaches about 0.7 V (the threshold voltage), and then rises steeply. In the reverse direction, the resistance is very high and essentially no current flows. The I–V graph shows current only on one side of the origin.

Straight line through origin = ohmic conductor (e.g. fixed resistor). Constant resistance.

Curve that flattens (symmetrical) = filament lamp. Resistance increases with temperature.

Current in one direction only = diode. Very high resistance in reverse.

In the exam you may be given a graph and asked to identify the component, or asked to sketch the I–V graph for a named component. Make sure you practise both.

Special Resistors: LDRs and Thermistors

Some components have a resistance that changes in response to the environment. These are useful in sensing circuits.

A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has a resistance that depends on light intensity. In bright light, the resistance of an LDR is low. In darkness, the resistance is high. LDRs are used in circuits that detect light levels — for example, automatic street lights that switch on when it gets dark.

A thermistor (in GCSE, this means an NTC thermistor) has a resistance that depends on temperature. As the temperature increases, the resistance of a thermistor decreases. As the temperature decreases, the resistance increases. Thermistors are used in temperature-sensing circuits — for example, thermostats that control central heating.

Key Fact

LDR: more light → lower resistance. Thermistor: higher temperature → lower resistance. Both are used in sensing circuits. Remember: for both components, the resistance goes down when the stimulus (light or heat) goes up.

In a filament lamp, the metal filament heats up as current flows. Hotter metal atoms vibrate more, creating more obstacles for the electrons — so resistance increases with temperature.

In a thermistor, the semiconductor material releases more charge carriers as it heats up, making it easier for current to flow — so resistance decreases with temperature.

In an LDR, photons of light release charge carriers in the semiconductor — more light means more carriers and lower resistance.

Charge Flow and Current

Current is linked to charge flow by the equation:

\(\text{charge flow} = current \times time\)

\(Q = I \times t\)

where Q is charge in coulombs (C), I is current in amperes (A), and t is time in seconds (s). One ampere means one coulomb of charge passes a point in the circuit every second.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions, always write the equation first, substitute the values with units, and show your working clearly. If asked to “explain” how the resistance of a filament lamp changes, link your answer to temperature: as current increases, the filament heats up, metal ions vibrate more, so resistance increases. For the required practical, be ready to describe the circuit, name the measuring instruments (ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel), and explain how you would obtain negative readings by reversing the connections.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • V = IR links potential difference (V), current (I) and resistance (R). Ohm’s law states current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature — true for ohmic conductors only.
  • I–V graphs show how components behave: straight line (resistor), curve (filament lamp), one-way flow (diode). Know how to sketch and identify each.
  • LDR resistance falls in bright light; thermistor resistance falls as temperature rises. Both are used in sensing circuits.

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
lessons.description: How current and voltage behave in series and parallel circuits, and calculating total resistance.
lessons.content_html:
Two Types of Circuit

Every electrical circuit you meet in GCSE Physics falls into one of two categories: series or parallel. Understanding how current, voltage, and resistance behave in each type is essential — the exam frequently tests whether you can apply the rules to unfamiliar circuits and perform calculations.

In a series circuit, all components are connected one after another in a single loop. There is only one path for the current to take. In a parallel circuit, the circuit splits into two or more branches, giving the current multiple paths. Most real-world circuits — including household wiring — use parallel connections.

Current in Series Circuits

In a series circuit, there is only one path for the current to flow through. This means the current is the same at every point in the circuit. It does not matter where you place an ammeter — before the first component, between the two, or after the last — the reading will always be identical.

Key Fact

In a series circuit, the current is the same everywhere: Itotal = I1 = I2 = I3

This happens because charge has no alternative route. Every coulomb of charge that leaves the cell must pass through every component before returning. If one component breaks, the entire circuit stops working because the single loop is broken.

Voltage in Series Circuits

Voltage (potential difference) behaves differently from current in a series circuit. The total voltage supplied by the cell is shared between the components. Each component uses up some of the energy carried by the charge, so the voltages across all components add up to the supply voltage.

Key Fact

In a series circuit, the voltages across components add up to the total supply voltage: Vtotal = V1 + V2 + V3

If two identical resistors are connected in series to a 6 V battery, each resistor gets 3 V across it. If the resistors are different, the one with the higher resistance takes a larger share of the voltage.

Resistance in Series Circuits

When resistors are connected in series, the total resistance is simply the sum of all the individual resistances. Adding more resistors in series increases the total resistance, which reduces the current flowing through the circuit.

Three resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω, and 10 Ω are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance.

Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 = 4 + 6 + 10 = \(20 \, \Omega\)

If the supply voltage is 12 V, the current can be found using Ohm’s law: I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6 A

Current in Parallel Circuits

In a parallel circuit, the current splits at each junction (branch point). The total current from the supply equals the sum of the currents through each branch. More current flows through the branch with the lower resistance.

Key Fact

In a parallel circuit, current is shared between branches: Itotal = I1 + I2 + I3

For example, if a parallel circuit draws 3 A from the supply and one branch carries 1.2 A, the other branch must carry 1.8 A. The current recombines after the branches and returns to the cell.

Voltage in Parallel Circuits

The voltage across each branch of a parallel circuit is the same as the supply voltage. This is because each branch is connected directly to the cell, so every component on every branch receives the full potential difference from the supply.

Key Fact

In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch equals the supply voltage: Vtotal = V1 = V2 = V3

This is why household appliances are wired in parallel — each device receives the full 230 V mains supply regardless of how many other devices are switched on.

Resistance in Parallel Circuits

Adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance of the circuit. This seems surprising, but it happens because each new branch provides an additional path for current to flow. The total resistance of a parallel combination is always less than the smallest individual resistor.

For two resistors in parallel, use the formula: 1 ÷ Rtotal = 1 ÷ R1 + 1 ÷ R2

Example: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel. Find the total resistance.

1 ÷ Rtotal = 1 ÷ 6 + 1 ÷ 12 = 2 ÷ 12 + 1 ÷ 12 = 3 ÷ 12

Rtotal = 12 ÷ 3 = \(4 \, \Omega\)

Notice that 4 Ω is less than the smallest individual resistor (6 Ω). This is always the case with parallel resistors.

Why Does This Matter?

Understanding these rules lets you predict what happens when components are added to or removed from a circuit. In a series circuit, adding more resistors increases total resistance and decreases current. In a parallel circuit, adding more branches decreases total resistance and increases total current from the supply.

Current: Same everywhere in series; splits between branches in parallel.

Voltage: Shared between components in series; the same across each branch in parallel.

Resistance: Total resistance increases in series (Rtotal = R1 + R2); total resistance decreases in parallel (always less than the smallest resistor).

If one component breaks: The whole circuit stops in series; other branches continue working in parallel.

Christmas tree lights are a classic example. Old-fashioned sets used series wiring — if one bulb blew, the whole string went dark. Modern sets use parallel wiring, so a single blown bulb does not affect the rest.

In exam questions, you may be given a circuit diagram and asked to identify whether components are in series or parallel, then apply the correct rules. Always start by tracing the path of the current: if there is only one loop, it is series; if the current splits, it is parallel.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to calculate total resistance, show your working clearly — write out the formula first, then substitute the values. For parallel resistance, remember to find 1 ÷ Rtotal first, then flip it to get Rtotal. A common mistake is forgetting the final step and leaving the answer as 1 ÷ Rtotal. For compare and explain questions about series vs parallel, always state the rule (e.g. “current is the same in series”) and then explain why (e.g. “because there is only one path for the charge to flow through”).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In a series circuit, current is the same everywhere and voltage is shared between components. Total resistance = R1 + R2 + R3.
  • In a parallel circuit, voltage is the same across each branch and current splits between branches. Total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistor.
  • Adding resistors in series increases total resistance and decreases current; adding branches in parallel decreases total resistance and increases total current.

lessons.title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
lessons.description: AC vs DC, the three-pin plug, fuses, power equations, and the National Grid.
lessons.content_html:
AC and DC — Two Types of Current

All electrical circuits carry current, but current can flow in two different ways. Understanding the difference between them is essential for this topic.

Direct current (d.c.) flows in one direction only. The current is constant in size and does not change direction. Batteries, cells, and solar cells all supply d.c. If you plotted d.c. on a voltage–time graph, you would see a flat horizontal line above the axis.

Alternating current (a.c.) repeatedly changes direction. The current flows back and forth, and the potential difference alternates between positive and negative values. The UK mains electricity supply is a.c. with a frequency of 50 Hz and a potential difference of about 230 V. This means the current completes 50 full cycles every second.

Key Fact

UK mains supply: a.c., 230 V, 50 Hz. Batteries supply: d.c. These three facts come up repeatedly in exam questions.

On an oscilloscope, a.c. appears as a smooth wave that rises above and falls below the centre line. The peak voltage is measured from zero (the centre line) to the top of the wave. D.c. appears as a straight, flat line above the centre line. If the exam gives you two traces and asks which is a.c. and which is d.c., look for the wave shape versus the flat line.

The Three-Pin Plug

Most electrical appliances in the UK connect to the mains through a three-pin plug. Inside the plug there are three colour-coded wires, a fuse, and a cable grip. You need to know what each part does.

Live wire (brown): The live wire carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. Its potential difference keeps swapping between positive and negative. It is about 230 V compared with earth. This is the dangerous wire — even when an appliance is switched off, the live wire can still be at 230 V.

Neutral wire (blue): The neutral wire completes the circuit. It is at, or close to, 0 V (earth potential). Current flows in through the live wire and out through the neutral wire.

Earth wire (green and yellow): The earth wire is a safety wire. It does not carry current during normal operation. If a fault causes the metal casing of an appliance to become live, the earth wire provides a low-resistance path for current to flow safely to earth, which causes the fuse to blow and breaks the circuit.

Key Fact

Live = brown (dangerous, ~230 V). Neutral = blue (0 V, completes circuit). Earth = green/yellow (safety, connected to metal casing). A common exam mistake is mixing up the wire colours — remember: Brown = Live (Bottom Right), Blue = Neutral (Bottom Left).

Electrical Safety — Fuses and Circuit Breakers

Electrical faults can be dangerous. If the current flowing through an appliance becomes too large, wires overheat, which can cause fires. Two devices protect against this: fuses and circuit breakers.

A fuse is a thin piece of wire inside a ceramic or glass casing. When the current exceeds the fuse’s rated value, the wire heats up, melts, and breaks the circuit. Fuses are fitted inside the plug, on the live wire side. Common fuse ratings are 3 A, 5 A, and 13 A. Once a fuse has “blown” it must be replaced — it cannot be reused.

To select the correct fuse, calculate the normal operating current of the appliance using P = I × V, then choose a fuse with a rating just above that value. For example, a 700 W microwave on a 230 V supply draws about 3.04 A, so a 5 A fuse is correct. A 3 A fuse would blow during normal use; a 13 A fuse would allow a dangerously large current before breaking the circuit.

A circuit breaker does the same job as a fuse but works differently. It is an electromagnetic switch that trips (opens) when the current is too large. Unlike a fuse, a circuit breaker can be reset by flipping it back — there is no wire to replace. Circuit breakers also react faster than fuses, which makes them safer. Modern consumer units (fuse boxes) in homes use circuit breakers rather than fuses.

Key difference for the exam: Fuses melt and must be replaced. Circuit breakers trip and can be reset. Both break the circuit when current is too high. Neither protects against electrocution on its own — that requires an RCD (residual current device), which detects a difference in current between the live and neutral wires.

Key Fact

Fuses prevent fires, not electrocution. It only takes about 0.1 A to stop a human heart, but a 3 A fuse would not blow at such a low current. The earth wire works with the fuse — a fault causes a surge of current through the earth wire, which blows the fuse and disconnects the supply.

Power Equations

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred. It is measured in watts (W), where 1 W means 1 joule of energy transferred per second. Two key equations link power to other electrical quantities:

Equation 1: P = I × V — Power (W) equals current (A) multiplied by potential difference (V).

Equation 2: P = I² × R — Power (W) equals current squared (A²) multiplied by resistance (Ω). This version is useful when you do not know the voltage.

Example 1: A kettle operates at 230 V and draws a current of 10 A. Calculate its power. P = I × V = 10 × 230 = 2300 W (2.3 kW).

Example 2: A lamp has a power rating of 60 W and is connected to the 230 V mains. What current does it draw? Rearrange P = I × V to give I = P ÷ V = 60 ÷ 230 = 0.26 A. A 3 A fuse would be appropriate.

Energy Transferred

The amount of energy transferred by an appliance depends on its power and how long it is used for. The equation is:

\(E\,=\,P\, \times \,t\) — Energy transferred (J) equals power (W) multiplied by time (s). This can also be written as E = I × V × t by substituting P = I × V.

For example, a 2000 W heater left on for 5 minutes transfers E = 2000 × 300 = 600,000 J (600 kJ). Always convert minutes to seconds before substituting into the equation.

The National Grid

The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers that links power stations to consumers across the UK. Electricity is generated at power stations, transmitted along high-voltage cables supported by pylons, and then delivered to homes and businesses.

The key challenge is efficiency. When current flows through cables, some energy is wasted as heat due to the resistance of the wires. The power lost as heat is given by P = I² × R. Because current is squared in this equation, even a small reduction in current leads to a large reduction in energy wasted.

Step-up transformers at power stations increase the potential difference from about 25,000 V to 400,000 V for transmission. Increasing the voltage means the current decreases (since power = voltage × current, and power stays roughly constant). Lower current means less energy is wasted heating the cables.

Step-down transformers near homes and businesses reduce the potential difference back down to 230 V, which is safe for domestic use. Without transformers, either the cables would need to be impossibly thick (to reduce resistance), or enormous amounts of energy would be wasted as heat.

Key Fact

The National Grid uses high voltage and low current for transmission to reduce energy losses. Power lost in cables = I² × R — halving the current reduces power loss to a quarter.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions, always show your working: write the equation, substitute the values, then give the answer with the correct unit. For “explain” questions about the National Grid, link your answer to the equation P = I² × R — state that step-up transformers increase voltage, which decreases current, which reduces energy lost as heat in the cables. Many students lose marks by saying “reduces energy loss” without explaining why (the I² relationship).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK mains supply is a.c. at 230 V, 50 Hz. Batteries supply d.c. The live wire carries the alternating p.d., the neutral is at 0 V, and the earth wire is a safety connection.
  • Fuses and circuit breakers protect against fires caused by excess current. Choose a fuse with a rating just above the normal operating current (calculated using P = I × V).

lessons.title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State
lessons.description: Density calculations, the particle model of states, and what happens during changes of state.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Density?

Density is a measure of how much mass there is in a given volume. A dense material has its particles packed closely together, so there is a lot of mass in a small space. A less dense material has its particles more spread out.

The equation for density is:

Key Fact

\(Density (\rho ) = mass (m) \div volume (V)\)
Units: density in kg/m³ (or g/cm³), mass in kg (or g), volume in m³ (or cm³).
You must be able to recall this equation.

You need to be able to rearrange this equation. To find mass: \(m = \rho \times V\). To find volume: \(V = m \div \rho\). For example, if an object has a mass of 500 g and a volume of 50 cm³, its density is 500 ÷ 50 = 10 g/cm³.

Measuring Density — Required Practical

You need to know how to measure the density of both regular and irregular solid objects, and you may be asked about this in the exam. The method depends on the shape of the object.

For a regular solid such as a cube or rectangular block:

1. Measure the mass using a digital balance.
2. Measure the length, width, and height using a ruler or vernier callipers.
3. Calculate the volume (length × width × height for a rectangular block).
4. Use the equation ρ = m ÷ V to calculate density.

For an irregular solid (e.g. a pebble or a key):

1. Measure the mass using a digital balance.
2. Fill a eureka can (displacement can) with water until it overflows from the spout.
3. Gently lower the object into the water. The water displaced by the object flows out of the spout and into a measuring cylinder.
4. Read the volume of displaced water from the measuring cylinder — this equals the volume of the object.
5. Use ρ = m ÷ V to calculate density.

The Particle Model of Matter

All matter is made up of tiny particles (atoms or molecules). The particle model explains the properties of the three states of matter — solid, liquid, and gas — in terms of how their particles are arranged and how they move.

Key Fact

Solids: Particles are held closely together in a fixed, regular arrangement. They vibrate about fixed positions but cannot move freely. Strong forces of attraction between particles. High density.
Liquids: Particles are close together but can slide past each other. Arrangement is irregular. Medium forces of attraction. Medium density.
Gases: Particles are far apart and move randomly at high speeds. Almost no forces of attraction. Very low density. Gases can be compressed because of the large spaces between particles.

The particle model explains why solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume, liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container, and gases have no fixed shape or volume — they spread out to fill any space available. It also explains density differences: solids are generally the densest state because their particles are packed most closely, while gases are the least dense because their particles are spread far apart.

Changes of State

When a substance is heated or cooled, it can change from one state to another. These changes are called changes of state. During a change of state, the substance’s mass is conserved — it stays the same because no particles are added or lost.

The key changes of state are:

Melting — solid to liquid. Happens at the substance’s melting point. Energy is absorbed to weaken the bonds between particles so they can move past each other.
Boiling — liquid to gas. Happens at the substance’s boiling point. Energy is absorbed to overcome the forces of attraction between particles so they can move freely.
Evaporation — liquid to gas, but it happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature below the boiling point. The most energetic particles at the surface escape into the gas phase.
Condensation — gas to liquid. Happens when a gas is cooled and particles lose energy and move closer together.
Freezing — liquid to solid. Happens at the freezing point (which is the same temperature as the melting point). Energy is released as particles form a fixed arrangement.
Sublimation — solid directly to gas, without passing through the liquid state.

Key Fact

A change of state is a physical change, not a chemical change. The substance can be reversed back to its original state. No new substance is formed, and the mass is conserved because the total number of particles stays the same.

When a substance is changing state (e.g. ice melting to water), the temperature remains constant even though energy is still being supplied. This is because the energy is being used to break or weaken the bonds between particles rather than increasing their kinetic energy. The energy absorbed during a change of state is called latent heat. On a heating curve, the flat sections (where temperature does not change) represent changes of state.

Internal Energy

Every object or system stores internal energy. Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system. When a substance is heated, its internal energy increases — the particles gain kinetic energy and move more vigorously. During a change of state, the potential energy of the particles changes (bonds break or form) but the kinetic energy stays the same, which is why the temperature does not change.

Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid, at any temperature. Only the fastest (most energetic) particles escape from the surface, which is why evaporation causes cooling — the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles decreases, so the temperature drops.

Boiling happens throughout the liquid, only at the boiling point. Bubbles of gas form inside the liquid and rise to the surface. Boiling requires a continuous energy input and happens at a fixed temperature for a given substance.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Density calculation questions are common on Physics Paper 1 — always show your working and include units. If the question asks you to describe the required practical, state the equipment used (balance, ruler, eureka can, measuring cylinder) and explain each step clearly. For “explain” questions about changes of state, always link your answer to particles: describe what happens to the arrangement, movement, and energy of particles. Remember that mass is conserved during a change of state — this is a common exam trap.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Density = mass ÷ volume (ρ = m/V). You must know how to measure density for regular shapes (ruler + balance) and irregular shapes (eureka can + balance).
  • The particle model explains why solids are dense with a fixed shape, liquids flow and take the shape of their container, and gases are easily compressed and spread to fill any space.
  • Changes of state (melting, boiling, evaporation, condensation, freezing, sublimation) are physical changes where mass is conserved, and temperature stays constant during the change because energy goes into breaking or forming bonds, not increasing kinetic energy.

practice_questions.text: A student heats a beaker of ice from −10 °C. Describe and explain what happens to the temperature and state of the water as it is heated from −10 °C to 120 °C. Include the names of the changes of state that occur.

• Temperature rises from 0 °C to 100 °C — water warms up, particles move faster, kinetic energy increases
• At 100 °C — boiling occurs (liquid to gas), temperature stays constant, energy is used to break bonds between particles (latent heat of vaporisation)
• Temperature rises above 100 °C — steam is heated further, gas particles gain kinetic energy
• Mass is conserved throughout because no particles are created or destroyed

Mid band (3-4): Describes the changes of state but explanation of constant temperature is limited or incomplete.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about heating/changes with little or no particle explanation.

lessons.title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
lessons.description: How heating changes internal energy, and calculations using SHC and specific latent heat equations.
lessons.content_html:
Internal Energy

Every substance is made up of particles (atoms or molecules) that are constantly moving. The internal energy of a system is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles within it. When you heat a substance, you transfer energy to its particles, increasing the internal energy of the system.

The kinetic energy of particles is related to their movement. In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions. In a liquid, they move more freely. In a gas, they move rapidly in all directions. Heating a substance makes the particles move faster, increasing their kinetic energy and raising the temperature.

Key Fact

Internal energy = total kinetic energy + total potential energy of all the particles. A rise in temperature means the particles have gained kinetic energy. A change of state means the particles have gained potential energy (their spacing changes) but the temperature stays the same.

Changes of State and Internal Energy

When a substance changes state (for example, from solid to liquid or liquid to gas), the energy being supplied does not increase the temperature. Instead, it is used to break or weaken the bonds between particles, increasing their potential energy. The particles move further apart, but their speed does not change, so the temperature remains constant during a change of state.

This is a crucial point for the exam: during a change of state, the temperature does not change even though energy is still being transferred. Once the change of state is complete, the temperature begins to rise again as kinetic energy increases.

A heating curve is a graph of temperature against time for a substance being heated steadily. It has a distinctive shape with five regions:

Region 1 — Solid heating: Temperature rises as the particles gain kinetic energy and vibrate faster. Region 2 — Melting (fusion): Temperature stays constant at the melting point while the solid changes to a liquid. Energy is used to overcome forces between particles (potential energy increases). Region 3 — Liquid heating: Temperature rises again as liquid particles gain kinetic energy. Region 4 — Boiling (vaporisation): Temperature stays constant at the boiling point while the liquid changes to a gas. Region 5 — Gas heating: Temperature rises as gas particles gain kinetic energy.

The flat sections on a heating curve are where changes of state happen. During these flat sections, the substance exists as a mixture of two states (e.g. solid and liquid during melting). All the energy supplied goes into changing the arrangement of particles, not into raising the temperature.

Specific Heat Capacity

Specific heat capacity (SHC) tells you how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C. Different materials have different specific heat capacities. Water has a high SHC of 4,200 J/kg °C, meaning it takes a lot of energy to heat up. Aluminium has an SHC of about 900 J/kg °C, so it heats up much more quickly.

The equation linking energy, mass, specific heat capacity, and temperature change is:

Key Fact

\(\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta \theta\) — where ΔE is the change in thermal energy (J), m is the mass (kg), c is the specific heat capacity (J/kg °C), and Δθ is the temperature change (°C). This equation is given on the physics equation sheet in the exam.

To use this equation, you need to be comfortable rearranging it. For example, to find the specific heat capacity: c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ). To find the temperature change: Δθ = ΔE ÷ (m × c). Always check your units — mass must be in kilograms, not grams.

Question: A 1 kg aluminium block is heated by a 50 W heater for 5 minutes. The temperature rises by 12.5 °C. Calculate the energy supplied and the specific heat capacity of aluminium.

Step 1 — Energy supplied: Power = 50 W, Time = 5 × 60 = 300 s. Energy = Power × Time = 50 × 300 = 15,000 J.

Step 2 — Specific heat capacity: ΔE = m × c × Δθ, so c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ) = 15,000 ÷ (1 × 12.5) = 1,200 J/kg °C.

Note: The accepted value for aluminium is about 900 J/kg °C. The experimental value is higher because some energy is lost to the surroundings rather than heating the block. Insulating the block with a lagging jacket would improve accuracy.

The SHC Required Practical

In the required practical, you determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block or water using an electrical heater. Key steps include: measuring the mass of the block (in kg), recording the starting temperature, switching on the heater for a set time, recording the final temperature, and calculating the energy supplied using E = P × t (where P is the power in watts and t is the time in seconds).

Common improvements to make the experiment more accurate include: wrapping the block in insulation to reduce thermal energy losses, waiting for the temperature to peak after switching off the heater before taking the final reading, and using a digital thermometer for more precise temperature measurements. The experimental value is usually too high because not all the electrical energy heats the block — some is lost to the surroundings.

Specific Latent Heat

When a substance changes state, the energy needed is described by the specific latent heat. There are two types:

Specific latent heat of fusion (Lf) is the energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from a solid to a liquid (or liquid to solid) at its melting point, without any change in temperature. For water, Lf = 334,000 J/kg.

Specific latent heat of vaporisation (Lv) is the energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from a liquid to a gas (or gas to liquid) at its boiling point, without any change in temperature. For water, Lv = 2,260,000 J/kg. Vaporisation requires much more energy than fusion because the particles must completely overcome the intermolecular forces to become a gas.

Key Fact

\(E = m \times L\) — where E is the energy (J), m is the mass (kg), and L is the specific latent heat (J/kg). This equation is given on the physics equation sheet. Use Lf for melting/freezing and Lv for boiling/condensing.

Question: How much energy is needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C? (Specific latent heat of fusion of water = 334,000 J/kg)

Solution: E = m × L = 0.5 × 334,000 = 167,000 J (or 167 kJ).

Question: A kettle supplies 452,000 J of energy to boil water. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2,260,000 J/kg. What mass of water is turned into steam?

Solution: m = E ÷ L = 452,000 ÷ 2,260,000 = 0.2 kg (200 g).

Linking It All Together

When you heat a substance from one state to another, you may need to use both equations in sequence. For example, to heat ice from −10 °C to steam at 100 °C, you would calculate: (1) the energy to heat the ice from −10 °C to 0 °C using ΔE = mcΔθ, (2) the energy to melt the ice at 0 °C using E = mLf, (3) the energy to heat the water from 0 °C to 100 °C using ΔE = mcΔθ, and (4) the energy to boil the water at 100 °C using E = mLv. Each stage requires a separate calculation, and the total energy is the sum of all four.

During melting (fusion), the particles only need to partially overcome the forces holding them in a fixed structure. They remain close together but can now slide over each other. During boiling (vaporisation), the particles must completely overcome all intermolecular forces and move far apart. This requires much more energy. For water, Lv is roughly seven times larger than Lf, reflecting the much greater separation of particles when forming a gas.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions on SHC and latent heat, always show your working clearly — you can pick up method marks even if your final answer is wrong. Remember that mass must be in kg (divide grams by 1,000) and that both equations (ΔE = mcΔθ and E = mL) are given on the equation sheet. For “explain” questions about heating curves, state clearly that temperature stays constant during a change of state because energy is being used to overcome forces between particles (increasing potential energy) rather than increasing kinetic energy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all particles. Heating increases internal energy — either raising temperature (kinetic energy) or causing a change of state (potential energy).
  • Use ΔE = mcΔθ for temperature changes and E = mL for changes of state. Both equations are provided in the exam — practise rearranging them and converting units.
  • During a change of state the temperature remains constant because energy goes into breaking bonds between particles, not into making them move faster.

lessons.title: Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Half-Life
lessons.description: Atomic structure, types of nuclear radiation, decay equations and half-life calculations.
lessons.content_html:
The Structure of the Atom

Every atom has the same basic structure: a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre, surrounded by electrons orbiting in energy levels (shells). The nucleus contains two types of subatomic particle — protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons are negatively charged and orbit at relatively large distances from the nucleus.

An atom has a radius of about 1 × 10−10 m. The nucleus is around 10,000 times smaller than the atom itself, with a radius of about 1 × 10−14 m. Despite its tiny size, the nucleus contains almost all the atom’s mass. Most of the atom is empty space.

Key Fact

The atomic number (bottom number on the periodic table) tells you the number of protons. The mass number (top number) tells you the total number of protons and neutrons. Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

Isotopes

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons, but carbon-12 has 6 neutrons while carbon-14 has 8. Some isotopes have unstable nuclei — these are radioactive isotopes. They decay by emitting radiation to become more stable.

Types of Nuclear Radiation

When an unstable nucleus decays, it can emit one or more types of nuclear radiation. There are three main types you need to know for combined science: alpha (α), beta (β) and gamma (γ).

An alpha particle is made up of 2 protons and 2 neutrons — identical to a helium nucleus. It is the largest and most ionising type of radiation, but the least penetrating. Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air. When an atom emits an alpha particle, its mass number decreases by 4 and its atomic number decreases by 2.

A beta particle is a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus. It forms when a neutron splits into a proton and an electron — the electron is ejected at high speed. Beta particles are moderately ionising and moderately penetrating — they pass through paper but are stopped by a thin sheet of aluminium. When beta decay occurs, the mass number stays the same but the atomic number increases by 1.

Gamma radiation is an electromagnetic wave, not a particle. It has no mass and no charge. Gamma rays are the most penetrating type of radiation — they can only be reduced (not fully stopped) by several centimetres of lead or metres of concrete. However, they are the least ionising. Gamma emission does not change the mass number or atomic number of the nucleus.

Key Fact

There is a trade-off between ionising power and penetration: alpha is the most ionising but least penetrating, gamma is the most penetrating but least ionising, and beta sits in between for both properties.

Radioactive Decay Equations

Radioactive decay is a random process — you cannot predict exactly when a particular nucleus will decay. However, you can represent what happens using nuclear equations. In every nuclear equation, both the mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance on each side.

Alpha decay example: When uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay, it loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons. The uranium atom becomes thorium-234:

23892U → 23490Th + 42He

Beta decay example: When carbon-14 undergoes beta decay, a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton and emits an electron. Carbon-14 becomes nitrogen-14:

146C → 147N + 0−1e

Key Fact

In alpha decay, mass number drops by 4 and atomic number drops by 2. In beta decay, mass number stays the same and atomic number increases by 1. In gamma emission, neither number changes — the nucleus just loses energy.

Half-Life

The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve. It can also be defined as the time for the count rate (or activity) to fall to half its original value. Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.

Different isotopes have very different half-lives. Some, like uranium-238, have half-lives of billions of years. Others decay in fractions of a second. The key skill for exams is using half-life to calculate how activity changes over time.

A sample has an activity of 8000 Bq. After 30 days, the activity has fallen to 1000 Bq. What is the half-life?

Step 1: Count the number of halvings: 8000 → 4000 → 2000 → 1000 = 3 half-lives.

Step 2: Divide the total time by the number of half-lives: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 days.

Contamination and Irradiation

Contamination occurs when radioactive material gets onto or inside a person or object. This is dangerous because the radioactive atoms remain in contact with the body, continuing to emit radiation. Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an external source — the person does not become radioactive themselves.

The key difference matters for safety: contamination is more dangerous because you cannot move away from the source, whereas with irradiation the risk drops as soon as the source is removed or you move further away. Workers who handle radioactive materials take precautions such as wearing protective clothing, using tongs to increase distance from sources, and keeping exposure time as short as possible.

Key Fact

Contamination = radioactive material is on you or inside you (ongoing exposure). Irradiation = you are exposed to radiation from a distance (exposure stops when source is removed). A person who has been irradiated does not become radioactive.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing nuclear decay equations, always check that both the mass numbers (top) and atomic numbers (bottom) balance on each side. For half-life calculations, the easiest method is to keep halving the activity until you reach the target value, then count the number of halvings. Remember the difference between contamination and irradiation — this is a very common exam question and students often mix them up.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atoms have a small, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells. Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons — some are unstable and radioactive.
  • The three types of nuclear radiation — alpha, beta and gamma — differ in their composition, ionising power, penetrating ability and effect on the nucleus.
  • Half-life is the time for the number of unstable nuclei (or count rate) to halve. Contamination means radioactive material is on or inside you; irradiation means exposure from an external source.

lessons.title: Static Electricity and Electric Fields
lessons.description: How static charge builds up, dangers and uses of static, and electric field patterns.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Static Electricity?

All matter is made of atoms, and atoms contain positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons. Normally, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the overall charge is zero. static electricity occurs when electrons are transferred from one material to another, giving each material an overall charge.

Key Fact

Only electrons move when objects become charged — protons are fixed inside the nucleus and cannot transfer between materials. An object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged; an object that loses electrons becomes positively charged.

How Does Static Charge Build Up?

Static charge builds up when two insulating materials are rubbed together. The friction causes electrons to transfer from one surface to the other. For example, when a polythene rod is rubbed with a woollen cloth, electrons move from the wool onto the rod. The rod gains extra electrons and becomes negatively charged, while the cloth loses electrons and is left with an equal positive charge.

The opposite happens with an acetate rod: when rubbed with a cloth, electrons move from the rod onto the cloth. The rod loses electrons and becomes positively charged, and the cloth gains a negative charge.

Conductors, like metals, allow electrons to flow freely through them. If charge builds up on a conductor, the electrons simply flow away. Insulators do not allow charge to flow, so the electrons that are transferred by friction stay on the surface and build up. This is why you get a shock when you touch a metal door handle after walking on a nylon carpet — the charge that has built up on you is suddenly discharged through the conductor.

Attraction and Repulsion

Once objects are charged, they exert non-contact forces on each other. Two objects carrying the same type of charge (both positive or both negative) repel each other. Two objects carrying different types of charge (one positive and one negative) attract each other.

Key Fact

Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. A charged object can also attract small uncharged objects (such as pieces of paper) because it causes the electrons on the surface of the uncharged object to rearrange — a process called electrostatic induction.

The Van de Graaff Generator

The Van de Graaff generator is a device used to demonstrate static electricity. A moving rubber belt carries electrons away from the metal dome. The dome loses electrons and builds up a large positive charge. Because the dome is insulated from the ground, the charge cannot escape.

A rubber belt moves continuously inside the generator. At the bottom, friction between the belt and a roller transfers electrons onto the belt. As the belt moves upward, a metal comb near the dome removes electrons from the dome surface. The electrons travel down through a wire and are neutralised at the base. This leaves the dome with a growing positive charge.

When a person touches the dome, the charge spreads across their body. Because each strand of hair receives the same positive charge, the hairs repel each other and stand on end. If the charge on the dome becomes large enough, the potential difference between the dome and the earth becomes so great that a spark jumps across the gap — this is called sparking.

Dangers of Static Electricity

Static electricity can be dangerous in certain situations. When fuelling an aircraft or filling a car with petrol, friction between the flowing fuel and the pipe can cause a build-up of charge. If a spark occurs near the fuel vapour, it could cause an explosion or fire. Lightning is another example — the friction between ice crystals and water droplets inside storm clouds causes a massive build-up of charge, and the resulting spark (lightning bolt) can be lethal.

earthing is the main way to prevent dangerous static discharge. A conducting strap or wire connects the object to the ground. This provides a path for electrons to flow safely to or from the earth, preventing charge from building up. Fuel tankers, for example, have earthing straps that touch the ground to discharge any static before the fuel is transferred.

Uses of Static Electricity

Static electricity is not always a hazard — it has several practical applications. In spray painting, the paint droplets are given a charge and the object being painted is given the opposite charge (or is earthed). The droplets are attracted evenly to the surface, producing a smooth, even coat with less waste. The same principle is used in crop sprayers to ensure pesticide reaches all parts of a plant.

In photocopiers and laser printers, a drum is given a pattern of static charge that matches the image. Toner powder (which carries the opposite charge) sticks to the charged areas and is then transferred onto paper. Electrostatic precipitators in power station chimneys use charged plates to attract soot and ash particles out of waste gases before they reach the atmosphere.

Electric Fields

A charged object creates an electric field in the space around it. Any other charged object placed in this field will experience a non-contact force — either attraction or repulsion. The electric field is strongest close to the charged object and gets weaker with distance.

Key Fact

Electric field lines are drawn with arrows showing the direction a positive charge would move. Field lines point away from positive charges and towards negative charges. The closer together the field lines, the stronger the field at that point.

Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, the electric field is uniform — the field lines are equally spaced and parallel. Between two point charges (one positive, one negative), the field lines curve from the positive charge towards the negative charge. Between two like charges, the field lines repel and curve away from each other.

The concept of an electric field explains how charged objects exert forces on each other without touching. When a charged object is placed in another object’s electric field, the field exerts a force on it. The closer the objects, the stronger the force. This is why sparking occurs when the potential difference is high enough — the electric field between the charged object and a nearby earthed conductor is strong enough to ionise the air molecules, creating a conducting path for the charge to flow through.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on static electricity, always state which particles move (electrons, not protons) and in which direction. For “Explain” questions, link cause to effect clearly: friction causes electron transfer → one object gains electrons → becomes negatively charged. When drawing electric field lines, remember three rules: lines never cross, arrows point away from positive and towards negative, and closer lines mean a stronger field. For extended response questions, structure your answer with a clear opening statement, supporting points with scientific vocabulary, and a concluding link back to the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Static charge is caused by the transfer of electrons between insulating materials through friction — only electrons move, and the material gaining electrons becomes negative while the one losing electrons becomes positive.
  • Static electricity can be dangerous (sparks near fuel, lightning) but is prevented by earthing, and has useful applications including spray painting, photocopiers, and electrostatic precipitators.
  • An electric field surrounds every charged object — field lines show direction (away from positive, towards negative) and density of lines shows field strength.

lessons.title: Gas Pressure and Pressure in Fluids
lessons.description: Gas pressure, Boyle’s law, pressure in fluids, atmospheric pressure, and upthrust.
lessons.content_html:
Gas Pressure and the Particle Model

Gases are made up of tiny particles that move rapidly in random directions. When these particles collide with the walls of their container, they exert a force on the surface. The total force per unit area created by billions of these collisions is what we measure as gas pressure. This is a key idea for understanding how gases behave when conditions change.

Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². You may also see kilopascals (kPa) used, where 1 kPa = 1000 Pa.

Key Fact

Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of their container. The more frequent or forceful the collisions, the higher the pressure.

The Effect of Temperature on Gas Pressure

When a gas is heated in a sealed container (constant volume), the particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. Faster-moving particles hit the container walls more frequently and with greater force. Both effects increase the gas pressure.

This explains everyday observations. For example, an aerosol can warns against heating because the increased pressure inside the sealed container could cause it to explode. Conversely, if a gas is cooled, its particles slow down, collisions become less frequent and less forceful, and the pressure drops.

A sealed container of gas is at 20 °C and has a pressure of 100 kPa. Explain what happens to the pressure if the gas is heated to 80 °C.

Answer: Heating the gas increases the kinetic energy of the particles (1). They move faster and collide with the container walls more frequently (1) and with greater force (1). Since the volume is fixed, the pressure increases (1).

Gas Pressure and Volume — Boyle’s Law

For a fixed mass of gas at a constant temperature, increasing the volume of the container means the particles have more space to travel before hitting the walls. Collisions become less frequent, so the pressure decreases. Decreasing the volume has the opposite effect — particles are closer together, collisions are more frequent, and the pressure increases.

This inverse relationship is described by Boyle’s law:

Key Fact — Boyle’s Law

pV = constant (at constant temperature). If pressure increases, volume decreases proportionally, and vice versa. The equation to use is: \(p_{1}V_{1} = p_{2}V_{2}\).

A gas occupies a volume of 0.040 m³ at a pressure of 200 kPa. The gas is compressed at constant temperature until its volume is 0.010 m³. Calculate the new pressure.

Step 1: Write out Boyle’s law: p1V1 = p2V2

Step 2: Substitute: 200 × 0.040 = p2 × 0.010

Step 3: Solve: p2 = (200 × 0.040) ÷ 0.010 = 8.0 ÷ 0.010 = 800 kPa

The volume decreased by a factor of 4, so the pressure increased by a factor of 4 — this confirms the inverse relationship.

Pressure in Fluids

A fluid is any substance that can flow — this includes both liquids and gases. A fluid at rest exerts pressure on any surface in contact with it. This pressure acts in all directions at any given point in the fluid.

The pressure in a fluid increases with depth. This is because the deeper you go, the greater the weight of the column of fluid above you. The equation for calculating pressure due to a column of liquid is:

Key Fact — Pressure in a Column of Liquid

\(p = h \times \rho \times g\), where p = pressure in pascals (Pa), h = height of the column in metres (m), ρ = density of the liquid in kg/m³, and g = gravitational field strength in N/kg (on Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg).

This equation tells us three factors that affect pressure in a liquid: the depth (height of the column), the density of the liquid, and the gravitational field strength. A denser liquid (such as mercury compared to water) produces a higher pressure at the same depth. Similarly, a greater depth means a taller column of liquid pressing down, creating more pressure.

Calculate the pressure exerted at the bottom of a swimming pool that is 2.5 m deep. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg.

Step 1: Write the equation: p = h × ρ × g

Step 2: Substitute: p = 2.5 × 1000 × 9.8

Step 3: Calculate: p = 24,500 Pa (or 24.5 kPa)

Atmospheric Pressure

Atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the weight of the air above a surface. At sea level, atmospheric pressure is approximately 101 kPa (about 101,325 Pa). The atmosphere is a thin layer of gas attracted to the Earth by gravity.

As altitude increases, atmospheric pressure decreases. This is because at higher altitudes there is a shorter column of air above you, so there is less weight of air pressing down. The density of the atmosphere also decreases with altitude because gravity pulls gas molecules closer to the Earth’s surface, meaning fewer molecules are present at higher altitudes.

Key Fact

Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because there is less air above to exert a downward force. At sea level it is about 101 kPa; on a mountaintop it is significantly lower.

You can think of atmospheric pressure as the result of the same p = hρg relationship but applied to the column of air above you. The atmosphere does not have a clear boundary — it gradually thins out into space. This is why there is no sudden edge where atmospheric pressure drops to zero.

Upthrust and Floating

Upthrust is an upward force that acts on any object placed in a fluid. It is caused by the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the object. Because pressure increases with depth, the bottom of the object experiences a greater pressure (and therefore a greater force) than the top.

The result is a net upward force — the upthrust. Whether an object sinks or floats depends on how the upthrust compares to the object’s weight:

If the weight of the object is greater than the upthrust, the object sinks. This happens when the object is denser than the fluid it is placed in. If the weight is equal to the upthrust, the object floats. This happens when the object displaces a volume of fluid whose weight matches its own weight.

For example, a steel ship floats despite steel being denser than water because the hull is shaped to displace a large volume of water. The upthrust from this displaced water is enough to support the ship’s weight. A solid steel ball, however, sinks because it displaces a much smaller volume of water relative to its weight.

Consider a cube submerged in water. The pressure on the bottom face is greater than the pressure on the top face because the bottom is deeper. Since pressure = force ÷ area, and the top and bottom faces have the same area, the force on the bottom face is greater than the force on the top face. This difference in force is the upthrust.

The sideways pressures on the left and right (and front and back) faces are equal and opposite, so they cancel out. Only the vertical pressure difference produces a net force — the upthrust acting upward.

Key Fact

An object floats when the upthrust equals its weight. An object sinks when its weight exceeds the upthrust. Upthrust is caused by the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the object in a fluid.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For calculation questions using p = hρg, always check your units — h must be in metres, ρ in kg/m³, and g in N/kg to get pressure in pascals. For “explain” questions about gas pressure, always refer to particles, collisions, and force — a good answer shows that you use the particle model, not just say “pressure goes up.” For Boyle’s law calculations, write out p1V1 = p2V2 and substitute carefully before rearranging.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gas pressure is caused by particle collisions with container walls — increasing temperature or decreasing volume increases collision frequency and force, raising pressure. Boyle’s law: pV = constant at constant temperature.
  • Pressure in a liquid increases with depth and depends on density and gravitational field strength: p = hρg. Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because there is less air above.
  • Upthrust is the upward force on an object in a fluid, caused by the pressure difference between its top and bottom. An object floats when upthrust equals weight; it sinks when weight exceeds upthrust.
